title: The Year of Delegations
year: 9 AH — 630-631 CE, with arrivals continuing into 10 and 11 AH
teaser: They stopped fighting him and started arriving instead: more than seventy delegations at one mud-brick mosque.

layers.title: The Setting
layers.subtitle: Arabia had been waiting to see who won
layers.content:
Amr bin Salamah remembered exactly what the Arabs had been doing for twenty years. His people camped by a spring on a travelled road, and whenever a rider came through they would ask what was happening with that man. He claims Allah has revealed such and such, the riders said. And the Arabs, he said, left their Islam up to the conquest. Their position was: leave him alone to face his own people. If he is a truthful Prophet, he will overcome them.

Makkah fell. The waiting ended.

The arithmetic is the clearest way to see it. Ten thousand men marched on Makkah in 8 AH. Under a year later, thirty thousand marched to Tabuk. At the Farewell Pilgrimage the reports give either a hundred thousand or a hundred and forty-four thousand pilgrims — the sources do not agree on the figure, only on the scale.

He did not wait for any of it to arrive on its own. As soon as the new moon of Muharram appeared in the ninth year he sent men out: Uyainah bin Hisn to Bani Tamim, Adi bin Hatim to Tai' and Bani Asad, al-Ala' bin al-Hadrami to Bahrain, Ziyad bin Labid to Hadramawt, al-Muhajir bin Abi Umayyah to San'a', Ali bin Abi Talib to Najran to collect the sadaqah and the jizyah, and about a dozen others besides. Some went in Muharram; some were sent later, once the tribe they were going to had already converted.

Then the traffic reversed. The compilers of the Prophet's expeditions count more than seventy delegations coming into Madinah. Not all of them belonged to this year — Abdul-Qais had first come in or before 5 AH, and Daws arrived in early 7 AH while he was at Khaybar. But the flood was after Tabuk, and it was so distinct that Arabic historiography gave the year its own name.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari — Amr bin Salamah: 'the Arabs left their Islam up to the conquest'
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: What Happened
layers.subtitle: A poetry contest, then six men and an idol
layers.content:
Bani Tamim came the hard way. They had been urging tribes to stop paying the head tax, and had stopped themselves, so fifty horsemen under Uyainah bin Hisn rode by night, camped hidden by day, and took eleven men, twenty-one women and thirty boys in the desert. Ten of their leaders came to his door in Madinah calling him out. He talked with them, prayed Dhuhr, then sat in the courtyard of the mosque, where they announced they wished to boast. Their orator Utarid bin Hajib spoke; Thabit bin Qais bin Shammas answered for the Muslims. Their poet az-Zibriqan bin Badr recited; Hassan bin Thabit answered. When it was over al-Aqra' bin Habis said it out loud: their orator is better than ours and their poet is better than ours. They accepted Islam, and their women and children were given back.

Thaqif came in Ramadan of 9 AH, after Tabuk. Their chief Urwah bin Mas'ud had accepted Islam a year earlier and gone home confident, being a man more beloved to his people than their own firstborn sons; they shot him full of arrows and killed him. Months later, unable to hold out against neighbours who had all submitted, they sent six men, one of them the youngest, Uthman bin Abi al-As.

A tent was put up for them in a corner of the mosque so they could hear the Qur'an and watch the prayer. They asked for a treaty permitting them fornication, wine and usury; asked that their idol al-Lat be left standing; asked to be excused the prayer. Every request was refused. They went aside, conferred, and submitted. The single condition they got was that they would not have to pull al-Lat down themselves.

Khalid bin al-Walid was sent to do it. Al-Mughirah bin Shu'bah told his companions he would make them laugh at Thaqif, struck the idol and pretended to collapse. The watching Thaqif cried that the goddess had killed him. He got up and told them al-Lat was dirt and stones. They dug out its foundation and carried its jewels and garments back to Madinah.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Military Expeditions — the delegation of Bani Tamim
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Turning Point
layers.subtitle: Sixty Christians, one question, and an oath refused
layers.content:
Najran was not a tribe with a grievance. It was a country: a territory south of Makkah toward Yemen, seventy-three villages, a day's ride across, with a hundred thousand fighting men.

Sixty of them came in 9 AH. Twenty-four were of noble families and three of those ran the place: Abdul-Maseeh, al-Aqib, over administration and government; as-Sayyid, named al-Ayham or Shurahbil in the reports, over cultural and political affairs; and Abu Harithah bin Alqamah, the bishop, over everything religious.

They met him, exchanged questions, and refused Islam when he recited to them. Then came the question they had travelled for. What do you say about Isa?

He did not answer that day. The reply came as revelation: «إِنَّ مَثَلَ عِيسَىٰ عِندَ اللَّهِ كَمَثَلِ آدَمَ خَلَقَهُ مِن تُرَابٍ ثُمَّ قَالَ لَهُ كُن فَيَكُونُ» — 'Indeed, the likeness of Jesus before Allah is the likeness of Adam. He created him from dust, then said to him: Be — and he was.' (3:59) In the morning he told them what had been sent, then left them a day to think.

They still refused. So he offered what the same passage prescribed: «فَقُلْ تَعَالَوْا نَدْعُ أَبْنَاءَنَا وَأَبْنَاءَكُمْ» — come, let us call our sons and your sons, our women and your women, ourselves and yourselves, and invoke the curse of Allah upon the liars. (3:61)

He came out for it. Al-Hasan and al-Husayn were under his garment; Fatimah walked behind him. Seeing he was ready, the delegation withdrew to talk. Al-Aqib and as-Sayyid said it privately: we will not swear, because if he is truly a prophet and we exchange curses, neither we nor our descendants nor our animals survive it.

They came back and said they accepted his terms. He set the jizyah and two thousand garments, a thousand in Rajab and a thousand in Safar, each with an ounce of gold. In return they had the covenant of Allah and His Messenger and permission to practise their religion freely. They asked for a trustworthy man to receive it, and he sent Abu Ubaydah bin al-Jarrah.
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: The Revelation
layers.subtitle: One verse answered Najran, one closed the Ka'bah
layers.content:
Two revelations of that year did most of the work, and they pull in opposite directions — one settled how to live beside people who would not convert, the other ended an era at the Ka'bah.

The first was the Najran passage, 3:59-61. It did three things at once. It defined Isa by comparison with Adam, created without a father by a word. It forbade further dispute after knowledge. And it supplied a procedure — the mutual invocation of the curse — which was offered, declined, and never needed again. What replaced it was a signed arrangement: tax, garments, protection, and worship left alone. The Sealed Nectar notes what followed: Islam then spread in Najran on its own, and they stopped paying the tax that non-Muslims paid.

The second came in Dhul-Qa'dah or Dhul-Hijjah of the same year. Abu Bakr had been sent as deputy to lead the pilgrimage. Soon after the pilgrims left, the opening passages of Surat at-Tawbah were revealed: «بَرَاءَةٌ مِنَ اللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ إِلَى الَّذِينَ عَاهَدْتُمْ مِنَ الْمُشْرِكِينَ» — a declaration of freedom from obligation, from Allah and His Messenger, toward those idolaters with whom you had made a treaty. (9:1) Ali bin Abi Talib was sent to announce it, and caught up with Abu Bakr at al-Arj or Dajnan; asked whether he had come to take command, he said he had come only to make the proclamation.

On the day of sacrifice Ali stood at al-Jamrah and read it out: the treaties with the treaty-breaking idolaters were cancelled, with four months to reconsider; treaties honoured in full stood until they expired. Abu Bakr then had it announced that after this year no polytheist would perform the pilgrimage and nobody would circle the House unclothed.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari — Abu Bakr's pilgrimage of 9 AH and the proclamation at al-Jamrah
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

layers.title: What It Left Behind
layers.subtitle: Not everyone who arrived had actually come
layers.content:
Some who came were not delegations at all, only men with better information than their neighbours.

Adi bin Hatim had fled to Ash-Sham when Ali's raiding party demolished the idol of Tai'. His sister was taken captive, released with a mount, and told him this man had treated her better than her own father would have. So he came with no safe-conduct and no letter of protection. Sat before him, he was asked what he had run from. Did you flee so as not to say there is no god but Allah? Do you know another god? No, said Adi. Years later Adi reported the rest: that he had heard the Prophet ﷺ say a woman would one day travel alone from al-Hirah to circle the Ka'bah fearing nobody but Allah, and that the treasures of Kisra would be opened — and that he lived to see both.

Seventeen men of Bani Hanifah came in 9 AH, and one of them was Musaylimah bin Thumamah. He wanted to be made heir: if Muhammad appointed me his successor, he kept saying, I would be a Muslim. When the Prophet ﷺ came to him he was holding a piece of palm leaf, and he said: if you asked me for this, I would not give it to you. Musaylimah went home to Yamamah, declared himself a prophet in 10 AH, permitted wine and adultery, and was followed. He was killed at Yamamah in Rabi'ul-Awwal of 12 AH, under Abu Bakr, by Wahshi — the man who had killed Hamzah at Uhud.

The arrivals kept coming through the tenth year. The last was Nakh', two hundred men, in mid-Muharram of 11 AH.

Carry this, because the sirah is honest about it. Whole tribes had submitted; whole tribes had not yet changed. The Qur'an says so in the same breath as it praises them: «الْأَعْرَابُ أَشَدُّ كُفْرًا وَنِفَاقًا» — 'the bedouins are the harshest in disbelief and hypocrisy' (9:97) — and then, further on, «وَمِنَ الْأَعْرَابِ مَن يُؤْمِنُ بِاللَّهِ وَالْيَوْمِ الْآخِرِ» — 'and among the bedouins are those who believe in Allah and the Last Day.' (9:99) Arriving is not the same as being changed. The Book counted them separately, so should we.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari — Adi bin Hatim on the woman travelling alone from al-Hirah and the treasures of Kisra; the delegation of Bani Hanifah and Musaylimah
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (Ar-Raheeq Al-Makhtum), Darussalam

quiz.prompt: How many delegations do the compilers of the Prophet's expeditions count as having come to Madinah?

options.text: Twelve
More than seventy
Exactly a hundred
Three hundred and thirteen

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — The Delegations
quiz.scholar_reflection: The Sealed Nectar states that a detailed account of all of them is not possible and selects the ones of historical significance. Most, though not all, arrived after Tabuk.

quiz.prompt: The delegation of Thaqif asked for several concessions. Which one was granted?

options.text: Permission to keep drinking wine
Exemption from the prayer
That they would not have to demolish the idol al-Lat with their own hands
Permission to continue dealing in usury

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the Thaqif delegation
quiz.scholar_reflection: Everything touching law and worship was refused. The one thing conceded cost nothing: Khalid bin al-Walid was sent to pull the idol down instead, and al-Mughirah bin Shu'bah did the striking.

quiz.prompt: When the Prophet ﷺ offered the Najran delegation a mutual invocation of Allah's curse, what did they do?

options.text: They accepted, and the curse fell on their leaders
They declined, and agreed instead to a treaty with tribute and freedom of worship
They all accepted Islam on the spot
They left Madinah at night without answering

quiz.citation: Quran 3:61 and al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the Najran delegation
quiz.scholar_reflection: Their two chiefs reasoned privately that if he really was a prophet, exchanging curses would end them and their descendants. The agreement they took instead guaranteed their religion outright.

quiz.prompt: At the pilgrimage of 9 AH, who led the Muslims and who proclaimed the opening verses of Surat at-Tawbah?

options.text: The Prophet ﷺ led it himself and made the proclamation
Abu Bakr led the pilgrimage; Ali was sent to make the proclamation
Umar led it; Bilal made the proclamation
Ali led it and Abu Bakr made the proclamation

quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — Abu Bakr performs the pilgrimage; Sahih al-Bukhari
quiz.scholar_reflection: Abu Bakr asked Ali whether he had been put in command. Ali replied that he had been sent only to make the announcement, and the two continued the pilgrimage together.

quiz.prompt: Musaylimah of Bani Hanifah offered to accept Islam if he were made the Prophet's successor. What was he told?

options.text: That he would be given Yamamah to govern
That the matter would be decided by the Companions after the Prophet's death
That if he asked for the piece of palm leaf in the Prophet's hand, he would not be given it
Nothing — he was expelled from Madinah without a reply

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari, cited in al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the Bani Hanifah delegation
quiz.scholar_reflection: He went home, claimed prophethood in 10 AH, permitted wine and adultery, and was followed by his people. He was killed at Yamamah in 12 AH.

quiz.prompt: Thaqif were a whole city ready to submit, and their price was wine, usury, fornication, their idol and an exemption from prayer. All of it was refused. What do you make of that as negotiation?

options.text: Some things are not available at any level of demand
It risked losing them entirely, and he took the risk
Granting any of it would have made the religion a bargaining position
The one thing he did concede shows he distinguished substance from face-saving

quiz.slider_label: Meet them halfway — Refuse the whole list
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the Thaqif delegation
quiz.scholar_reflection: They went aside, realised there were no alternatives, and submitted. Then they went home and lied to their own people that terms had been imposed on them, because they were afraid to say they had agreed.

quiz.prompt: Al-Mughirah broke al-Lat by pretending to be struck dead first, so that Thaqif would see the goddess do nothing and then hear him laugh at it. What do you think of that method?

options.text: Fear of an idol dies faster from ridicule than from argument
It was a risk — mockery hardens people who are not ready
He showed them the emptiness rather than telling them about it
He was a man of Thaqif himself, which is why he could do it

quiz.slider_label: Argue it down — Show it is empty
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the destruction of al-Lat
quiz.scholar_reflection: They cried out that the goddess had killed him. He stood up and said al-Lat is nothing but a mass of dirt and stones, and then broke the door. The sirah records their astonishment when the foundations came out.

quiz.prompt: He came out for the mutual oath holding his two grandsons, with his daughter walking behind him. What does staking your own family on a claim mean to you?

options.text: It is the most expensive way there is of saying you are not bluffing
The verse named sons and women, so he brought exactly whom it named
It ended the argument without anyone having to lose it publicly
It reads as a test aimed at them, and they understood it

quiz.slider_label: Argue longer — Put it to the oath
quiz.citation: Quran 3:61 and al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the Najran delegation
quiz.scholar_reflection: Neither side ever swore. The bishops looked at a man walking out with his grandchildren and drew a conclusion, and the Christians of Najran kept their churches under written guarantee.

quiz.prompt: Delegations arrived in numbers only after Makkah fell and Tabuk succeeded. Does timing like that make a conversion less real?

options.text: People usually look at truth properly only once it stops being costly
Yes — much of it was politics, and the Qur'an itself says so
The early Muslims of Makkah are a different category, and everyone knew it
What a man starts with matters less than what he ends up with

quiz.slider_label: Suspect the late arrivals — Welcome the late arrivals
quiz.citation: Quran 9:97-99, and Sahih al-Bukhari — Amr bin Salamah on the Arabs waiting for the conquest
quiz.scholar_reflection: Uthman bin Abi al-As came in with the very last tribe to submit. During the apostasy wars he told them: you were the last to enter Islam, do not be the first to leave it. They stayed.

quiz.prompt: Adi bin Hatim came to Madinah with no safe-conduct, no letter and no guarantee, because his sister told him how she had been treated. What moved him, do you think?

options.text: One person's account of being treated well outweighed everything he had heard
He had already run out of anywhere to run to
Being asked what exactly he was fleeing from left him no answer
He was told his own religion was already inconsistent, and he knew it

quiz.slider_label: Convinced by argument — Convinced by conduct
quiz.citation: al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the mission to Tai' and the coming of Adi bin Hatim
quiz.scholar_reflection: His sister asked three times before she was granted anything, and was given a mount for the journey. Her sentence to her brother was that this man had done for her what her own father would not have done.
